parts.prompt: Bank of the float at byte offset 1000?

problems.title: Conflict degrees
problems.solution: The lanes hit banks $s\ell \bmod 32$; each bank is hit $\gcd(s, 32)$ times: 2, 8, 32, and 1 for any odd stride.

problems.title: Padding choices
problems.statement: A 32-row tile read by columns (lane ℓ reads row ℓ, column c), with row lengths of 32, 33 or 34 words.
hints: Column reads have stride equal to the row length.
problems.solution: gcd(32, 32) = 32, gcd(33, 32) = 1, gcd(34, 32) = 2. Padding works when it makes the row length odd.

problems.title: Cost of a conflicted transpose
problems.statement: A 32 × 8 block transposes a 32 × 32 unpadded tile; each thread reads 4 tile elements by column.
problems.solution: 4 instructions × 32 passes = 128, against 4 when padded: 32× fewer shared-memory cycles for one wasted column.

problems.title: Broadcasts
problems.statement: Same word: broadcast. Different words in the same bank: conflict.

parts.prompt: Lane ℓ reads word 32·(ℓ mod 2): passes?

problems.solution: (a) 16 distinct words in 16 distinct banks, each read by 2 lanes: 1 pass. (b) Two distinct words, both in bank 0: 2 passes. (c) Broadcast: 1.

problems.title: Fitting tiles
problems.statement: The GW-1 allows 48 KB of shared memory per block and 64 KB per SM, allocated in 256-byte chunks; at most 16 blocks per SM.

parts.prompt: Blocks per SM if each uses one such tile (shared memory only)?

hints: Round 4224 up to a multiple of 256.
problems.solution: (a) 4,224 bytes, (b) 4,352 (17 chunks), (c) $\lfloor 65536/4352 \rfloor = 15$ blocks: shared memory, not the 16-block limit, binds, by a hair.

problems.title: Swizzling instead of padding
problems.statement: Store element (r, c) of a 32 × 32 tile at word $32r + (c \oplus r)$ (XOR).

parts.prompt: Which layouts are conflict-free for both rows and columns?

hints: Column c, lane ℓ = row: bank $c \oplus \ell$, distinct for distinct ℓ.
problems.solution: (a) Row r: banks $c \oplus r$ for $c = 0..31$, a permutation. (b) Column c: banks $c \oplus \ell$, also a permutation. (c) Padding, XOR and rotation all work; XOR wastes no memory and suits power-of-two tiles, which is why CUTLASS and Triton use it.

problems.title: Barrier hazards

parts.prompt: Threads write a tile, then read neighbours' values from it…
options: without a barrier, since writes are fast

parts.prompt: A loop loads tile k, computes, then loads tile k+1 into the same buffer. It needs…
options: a barrier after the load and another before the next load overwrites it
a barrier only at the end

hints: Every thread must reach the same barrier; reads must finish before overwrites.
problems.solution: (a) A block-wide barrier between the writes and the reads; a barrier only some threads reach can deadlock, and __syncwarp covers only one warp. (b) Two: after loading (so reads see the data) and before overwriting (so slow readers finish). Forgetting the second is a classic race.

problems.title: Conflicts in time
problems.statement: A kernel issues 1,000,000 warp shared-memory loads, each with an average conflict degree of 8. Each SM serves one pass per cycle; the work is spread evenly over the GW-1's 16 SMs at 1.5 GHz.

parts.prompt: Time spent on shared-memory passes, in µs?

problems.solution: (a) $8 \times 10^6 / 16 = 500{,}000$ cycles = 333 µs. (b) 41.7 µs. Bank conflicts turn a memory-light kernel into an issue-bound one.

problems.title: What shared memory is for

parts.prompt: Which are good reasons to stage data in shared memory?
options: Turning a strided global access into coalesced ones (transpose)
Reusing a tile of data many times (tiled GEMM, stencils)
Exchanging values between threads of a block
Making a single coalesced streaming pass faster

hints: Shared memory pays off through reuse or reordering.
problems.solution: Reordering, reuse and communication. A single coalesced pass gains nothing from an extra copy, and registers are faster than shared memory for private values.
